title: Hacker Runs Hermes AI Agent Unattended for Post-Exploitation at Thai Finance Ministry

reading.body:
An attacker deployed an autonomous AI agent called Hermes to probe Thailand's Ministry of Finance network without human oversight after gaining initial access. The agent was left to operate unattended during post-exploitation, automating reconnaissance of the ministry's internal systems including its Hadoop cluster, mail infrastructure, and web applications. This represents a deployment of an AI system outside any human-in-the-loop control, allowing it to act on a compromised network for an extended period.

The attacker also created a custom malware implant named Hades to maintain persistence and exfiltrate data. Researchers discovered the operation through exposed files on a Hong Kong server containing exploit code, stolen credentials, and malware samples. The attack was detected and authorities were notified, though it is not established whether sensitive files were successfully stolen or what data the Hermes agent ultimately accessed.

This incident shows how AI agents designed for autonomous operation can be weaponized once a system is breached. The failure was not in the AI system's design but in its use as an attack tool. What would have stopped this is network segmentation and detection systems that flag autonomous agents making unexpected queries to sensitive infrastructure, since the agent's activity should have appeared as an anomaly compared to normal human access patterns.

summary:
# Summary

Thailand's Ministry of Finance was targeted in a cyberattack from July 9-13, 2026, involving attackers who exposed three directories on a Hong Kong server containing exploit code, stolen credentials, and malware. Researchers from Hunt.io and security journalist Bob Diachenko discovered 585 files totaling 470 MB that revealed the operator deployed an unnamed AI agent called Hermes to autonomously probe the ministry's network without human oversight. The attackers also created a custom implant named Hades, a Go-based malware in various disguises designed to maintain persistent access and communicate with command servers in Hong Kong and Malaysia.

The operation demonstrated detailed knowledge of the ministry's internal systems, including its Hadoop data cluster, mail infrastructure, and web applications. Attackers deployed custom scripts targeting these systems, including privilege escalation exploits and web shells. Session cookies and configuration files showed the operator accessed multiple ministry systems, though there is no confirmation that sensitive files were stolen. Thailand's cybersecurity authorities were notified on July 15, 2026, and acknowledged the report. The attack highlights a new trend where AI agents are being used to conduct espionage operations with minimal human involvement.
